name: Lemon
description: Lemon is an intensely acidic, non-climacteric botanical matrix belonging to the Rutaceae family, characterized by an ultra-concentrated profile of exogenous L-ascorbic acid and carboxylic acids. It serves as a specialized phytochemical delivery system rich in low-molecular-weight polymethoxyflavonoids and monoterpenes. This distinct biochemical complex acts as a powerful electron donor to mitigate intracellular oxidative stress, regulates the systemic acid-base equilibrium via alkaline metabolic residues, and modifies the enzymatic kinetics of the gastrointestinal tract.
macroIntro: The macronutrient infrastructure of lemon pulp presents a negligible energy density, featuring a highly diluted carbohydrate matrix balanced with structural dietary fibers and near-zero lipid or protein involvement.
microIntro: As a highly specialized post-harvest biochemical reservoir, lemon pulp concentrates water-soluble antioxidants, critical alkali metal ions, and volatile terpenes that act synergistically to modulate cellular signaling and renal excretion profiles.

macroNutrients.name: Calories
macroNutrients.description: An extremely low thermodynamic footprint that allows for broad metabolic integration without contributing to adipose tissue storage or altering insulin homeostasis.

macroNutrients.name: Protein
macroNutrients.description: Composed of trace fractions of structural plant proteins, yielding a negligible amino acid payload.

macroNutrients.name: Total Fat
macroNutrients.description: Virtually absent lipid profile, containing only minor structural membrane phospholipids.

macroNutrients.name: Carbohydrates
macroNutrients.description: Consists primarily of non-starch polysaccharides (pectin) alongside monosaccharide fragments, tightly bound within a high-acidity carboxylic matrix.

microNutrients.name: Vitamin C (L-Ascorbic Acid)
microNutrients.description: An essential reducing agent required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during procollagen synthesis, while actively scavenging free radicals.

microNutrients.name: Citric Acid
microNutrients.description: A fundamental tricarboxylic acid that drives salivary and gastric juice secretion kinetics, actively contributing to systemic alkalization after metabolic conversion.

microNutrients.name: Flavonoids (Hesperidin & Eriocitrin)
microNutrients.description: Specific citrus-derived glycosides that suppress the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway, decreasing endothelial cell permeability and capillary fragility.

microNutrients.name: Potassium
microNutrients.description: The primary intracellular cation, essential for maintaining transmembrane resting potential, counteracting sodium-induced hypervolemia, and regulating vascular tone.

microNutrients.name: Folate (Vitamin B9)
microNutrients.description: A critical coenzyme for one-carbon transfer reactions, driving purine and pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis required for rapid hematopoietic cell replication.

microNutrients.name: D-Limonene
microNutrients.description: A functional cyclic monoterpene that induces Phase II detoxification enzymes (such as glutathione S-transferase) and exhibits notable anti-inflammatory activities.

healthBenefits: Immune Cell Priming and Antioxidant Defense: High intracellular saturation with L-ascorbic acid enhances neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytic activity, while systematically regenerating endogenous alpha-tocopherol (Vitamin E) to prevent lipid peroxidation cascades.

Endothelial Protection and Microvascular Integrity: The synergistic combination of eriocitrin and potassium optimizes nitric oxide bioavailability in blood vessels, suppressing the transcription of vascular cell adhesion molecules and improving systemic microcirculation.

Renal Nephrolithiasis Prophylaxis: Absorbed citric acid undergoes hepatic oxidation to form bicarbonate ions, elevating urinary pH and total citrate excretion, which competitively inhibits the crystallization and precipitation of calcium oxalate stones.

Digestive Fluid Dynamics and Glycemic Control: The low pH of the organic matrix activates oral gustatory receptors, upregulating the secretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsin. Simultaneously, soluble pectin fibers delay gastric emptying, flattening postprandial glucose curves.
precautionsIntro: Due to its intensive carboxylic acid concentration and low pH value, the clinical incorporation of lemon demands strict screening under specific physiological conditions.
precautions: Gastroesophageal Reflux and Mucosal Irritation: The direct introductory low pH shifts gastric luminal acidity, which can relax the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and trigger immediate nociceptive pain receptors in patients with erosive esophagitis or GERD.

Enamel Demineralization and Surface Erosion: Prolonged contact with unbuffered lemon juice initiates the dissolution of hydroxyapatite crystals on the outer tooth surface. To prevent loss of enamel hardness, it is recommended to utilize a straw and rinse thoroughly with alkaline water without immediate brushing.

Exacerbation of Peptic Ulcerative Lesions: The high concentration of citric acid acts as a local chemical irritant on exposed submucosal layers, making it strictly contraindicated during the acute phases of gastric or duodenal ulcers due to the risk of inducing localized bleeding.

Immunological Cross-Reactivity and Hypersensitivity: Citrus proteins and specialized volatile compounds can act as direct allergens or haptenic triggers, inducing IgE-mediated cutaneous eruptions, contact dermatitis, or localized oral allergy syndrome (OAS) in susceptible individuals.
